newsitem.title: USA: GM chairman hopeful of settlement at parts plant.
newsitem.headline: GM chairman hopeful of settlement at parts plant.

text.p: Heading into another strike deadline with the United Auto Workers union on Friday night, General Motors Corp. Chairman Jack Smith said he remained hopeful the company can reach a new local contract without a walkout.
"They're still negotiating, hopefully they'll reach an agreement," Smith told reporters following the dedication of GM's Service Parts Operations' new $43 million world headquarters here.

About 5,300 workers from UAW Local 735 were poised to walk off the job at two Detroit-area transmission and component plants at 11:59 p.m. EDT (0359 GMT) Friday if a new local contract is not reached.
Union leaders at GM's Ypsilanti, Mich., Willow Run Powertrain plant want GM to add more workers, settle health and safety issues and limit the amount of work it sends to outside contractors.
The plant makes transmissions and related components for many of GM's front-wheel-drive and rear-wheel-drive cars and trucks.
A satellite facility in Romulus, Mich., also makes transmission parts. A strike at the two facilities would quickly ripple through GM's North American assembly and parts operations.

GM has been on a mission to make its manufacturing operations more efficient by not adding workers and letting its hourly work force shrink through attrition. Union leaders, who say their members are overworked, have resisted those efforts, leading to six strikes since the beginning of this year.

Pressed by reporters on Friday on GM's commitment to the Flint and Genesee County area, where the new parts operation is located, Smith said GM has no plans to abandon the area. But he said GM's operations here need to reach global competitive standards to survive.
"If we're not there, then we're going to lose. And when we lose, it means everyone losses," he said.

Analysts have said they expect GM to close its Buick City large car assembly plant. Smith reiterated on Friday that GM does not have any product plans for the Buick City large car assembly facility after 1999.

Although the demand for large cars shows no sign of picking up, he said GM is responding to strong truck demand by shifting some light truck assembly and medium-duty truck assembly work to its truck operations in the area.

"The trends in the marketplace will determine what happens," he said. "At the moment, trucks are selling very well and we're increasing our capacity and increasing our throughput in the plant to build trucks here."

The region was hard hit by layoffs and plant closings in the late 1980s, and became the focus of the movie "Roger and Me," in which GM was portrayed as an unfeeling industrial giant as filmmaker Michael Smith tried to get an interview with then-Chairman Roger Smith.

On other matters, Jack Smith said GM has undertaken a global manufacturing study so the company can keep its capacity balanced between developing markets such as South America and Asia, and mature markets such as the United States, Europe and Japan.

Located just south of Flint and about 50 miles north of Detroit, GM's new 300,000-square-foot Service Parts Operations headquarters houses 1,400 people who previously worked in two separate buildings.
Known as SPO, the unit sells replacement parts, accessories and service merchandising under the GM, ACDelco and Goodwrench Service names.
SPO has a total of 12,350 hourly and salaried workers in the United States, Canada, Mexico and 12 countries overseas.
GM stock fell 50 cents to $60.50 in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
